# Building a Doughnut Out of Two Circles: A Tour of Cubical Geometry

## The shape of a piece of string

Take a single piece of string. Hold one end in your left hand and the other
end in your right hand. As it lies between your hands, it is the simplest
geometric object imaginable: an *interval*, a line segment that begins at one
point and ends at another. Mathematicians call the idealized version of this
the **unit interval**, the set of all real numbers $t$ with $0 \le t \le 1$.
Its two endpoints, $0$ and $1$, are genuinely different places — you can pinch
them, label them, and tell them apart.

Now bring your two hands together and tie the ends into a loop. Something
remarkable has happened. The two endpoints, which a moment ago were distinct,
are now *the same point*. The string has become a circle. You did not add any
material; you did not stretch it; you simply declared that two points should be
treated as one. The geometry of the circle is born entirely from a single act
of **gluing**.

This little experiment is the seed of an entire modern viewpoint on geometry
and logic called **cubical type theory**. The central slogan is disarmingly
simple: *spaces are built from intervals, and the interesting structure lives
in how the endpoints are glued together.* A path is just a map out of an
interval. A loop is a path whose two ends land on the same spot. A surface is a
map out of a square. And complicated spaces — circles, doughnuts, spheres — are
assembled by recording, very explicitly, which boundary pieces of these basic
cubes are to be identified.

This article tells the story of a small, self-contained mathematical world in
which exactly this philosophy is carried out with complete precision. We will
build the circle from an interval, build the torus (the surface of a doughnut)
from a square, and then prove a clean and satisfying fact: **the torus is
nothing more than two circles multiplied together.**

## Gluing as a mathematical operation

The everyday word "gluing" hides a precise mathematical machine called a
**quotient**. Suppose you have a collection of points and a rule that says
which points should be regarded as the same. The quotient is the new collection
you obtain after honoring that rule — every group of "to-be-identified" points
collapses into a single new point, and everything else is carried along
untouched.

To build the circle, we start with the interval and impose exactly one gluing
rule:

$$\text{glue the point } 0 \text{ to the point } 1.$$

We write this rule as a relation: the point $0$ is *related* to the point $1$,
and to nothing else. Forming the quotient of the interval by this relation
produces a brand-new space. We call it the **Circle**. Every point of the
interval becomes a point of the circle, but the two former endpoints now
coincide. Their shared image is a distinguished point we call the **base
point**.

There is a canonical way to view the original interval sitting inside the
circle: the map that sends each interval point $t$ to its image in the circle.
This map is the **loop**. It is the formal embodiment of "running once around
the circle." And it satisfies precisely the property we engineered:

$$\text{loop}(0) = \text{base} = \text{loop}(1).$$

In words: the loop starts at the base point and ends at the base point. The two
endpoints of the string have been tied together. Nothing else has been
identified — every interior point of the loop is still its own distinct place
on the circle.

## How to use a circle: the recursion principle

Building a space is only half the job. The other half is knowing how to *use*
it — how to define functions out of it. Here cubical thinking offers an elegant
and rigid answer, and it is worth pausing on because it is the real engine of
the subject.

Suppose you want to define a function from the circle to some target collection
$X$. The circle was built from the interval by gluing, so a function out of the
circle is "the same as" a function out of the interval — **provided** that
function respects the gluing. Concretely:

> **Recursion principle for the circle.** To define a map from the circle to a
> set $X$, it suffices to give a map $f$ from the interval to $X$ together with
> a single proof that the two endpoints agree, $f(0) = f(1)$. This data induces
> a unique map out of the circle.

This is a contract. The map $f$ tells you where every point of the loop should
go. The equation $f(0) = f(1)$ is the toll you must pay for the gluing: since
the circle identified $0$ with $1$, any function out of the circle is obliged
to send them to the same place. Pay the toll, and you get your function.

Two computation rules describe how the resulting function behaves. At the base
point it returns $f(0)$, and along the loop at any point $t$ it returns $f(t)$.
In symbols, if $g$ is the induced map then $g(\text{base}) = f(0)$ and
$g(\text{loop}(t)) = f(t)$. There is also a **uniqueness** guarantee: any two
functions out of the circle that agree along the entire loop are in fact the
*same* function. There is no hidden freedom, no secret extra point you forgot
about — the loop sees everything. (Formally: the loop is *surjective*; every
point of the circle is $\text{loop}(t)$ for some $t$.)

This trio — *construct by gluing, compute on the generators, and pin down by
uniqueness* — is the rhythm of the entire theory. Once you internalize it for
the circle, the torus follows the same beat one dimension up.

## From string to fabric: the torus

A circle came from gluing the two ends of a one-dimensional interval. A torus
comes from gluing the edges of a two-dimensional **square**.

Picture a flat square sheet of rubber. Its boundary consists of four edges: a
bottom and a top (the horizontal pair), and a left and a right (the vertical
pair). Now perform two gluings:

1. **Glue the bottom edge to the top edge.** Rolling the sheet so its bottom
   meets its top turns the square into a cylinder — a tube.
2. **Glue the left edge to the right edge.** Bending the tube around so its two
   circular ends meet turns the cylinder into a doughnut.

The result is the **Torus**, the surface of a doughnut. As with the circle, we
never added material; we only declared identifications. Formally, we take the
square — the set of pairs $(x, y)$ where both coordinates lie in the unit
interval — and impose two gluing rules:

$$ (x, 0) \sim (x, 1) \quad\text{for every } x \qquad\text{(top to bottom)},$$
$$ (0, y) \sim (1, y) \quad\text{for every } y \qquad\text{(left to right)}.$$

The quotient by these two families of relations is the torus. There is a
canonical map sending each square point $(x,y)$ to its image on the torus, and
it satisfies exactly the two gluing equations we imposed: the bottom and top
edges coincide, and the left and right edges coincide.

The torus comes with its own recursion principle, in the same spirit as the
circle's but now demanding **two** tolls instead of one:

> **Recursion principle for the torus.** To define a map from the torus to a
> set $X$, it suffices to give a map $f$ from the square to $X$ together with
> two proofs: that $f$ agrees on the horizontal edges, $f(x,0) = f(x,1)$ for
> all $x$, and that $f$ agrees on the vertical edges, $f(0,y) = f(1,y)$ for all
> $y$. This data induces a unique map out of the torus.

Again there is a computation rule (the induced map sends the image of $(x,y)$
to $f(x,y)$) and a uniqueness guarantee (any map that agrees with $f$ on every
square point is *the* induced map). The square map is surjective: every point
of the torus is the image of some point of the square.

## The punchline: a doughnut is two circles

Here is where the construction pays a genuine dividend. There is an old and
beautiful intuition that the torus is a "product" of two circles. Think of how
you might address a point on a doughnut: you need to know *how far around the
big loop* you are (the longitude) and *how far around the tube* you are (the
meridian). Each coordinate is an angle — a point on a circle. So a point on the
torus is exactly a pair of circle-points. The torus *is* the circle times the
circle.

In our gluing model this intuition becomes a precise, verified theorem:

$$\boxed{\; \text{Torus} \;\simeq\; \text{Circle} \times \text{Circle}. \;}$$

The symbol $\simeq$ means **equivalence**: a perfect dictionary translating
back and forth between the two spaces with no information lost. The
construction of this dictionary is wholly explicit and uses only the recursion
principles we have already met.

Going *from the torus to the pair of circles* is the natural move. Take a point
on the torus, lift it to a representative square point $(x, y)$, and send it to
the pair $(\text{loop}(x), \text{loop}(y))$ — its longitude and its meridian.
This is well defined precisely because the loop already glues its own
endpoints: the toll on the torus's horizontal edges is paid by the circle's
identity $\text{loop}(0) = \text{loop}(1)$, and likewise for the vertical
edges. The gluings of the torus are *exactly* the gluings the two circles
already perform, so the map descends cleanly to the quotient.

Going *back, from a pair of circles to the torus*, we feed each circle
coordinate through the circle's recursion principle, nesting one inside the
other to assemble the square point and then map it into the torus. The two
tolls of the torus recursor are once more discharged by the circle's endpoint
identifications.

Finally one checks the two round-trips. Start on the torus, travel to the pair
of circles, and come home: you are exactly where you began. Start with a pair
of circles, travel to the torus, and come home: again, exactly where you began.
Both checks reduce, after unfolding the definitions, to bookkeeping that the
computation rules settle automatically. The dictionary is faithful in both
directions, and the equivalence is sealed.

## Why this matters

It would be easy to dismiss all of this as an elaborate way of saying something
obvious. But the value lies in the *method*, not just the conclusion. Three
ideas deserve emphasis.

**Spaces from instructions.** We never needed the real numbers' geometry,
distances, or continuity to make the circle and the torus behave like a circle
and a torus. We needed only an interval, a square, and a precise list of which
boundary pieces to identify. This is the cubical creed: geometry is a record of
gluing instructions, and those instructions can be written down with the same
rigor as an arithmetic identity. It is geometry rebuilt as algebra.

**Recursion as the universal interface.** Every one of our spaces came packaged
with a recursion principle — a single, uniform rule for defining maps out of
it, gated by exactly the equations that the gluing imposes. This is what makes
the constructions *composable*. To build the torus-to-circles map we did not
reach into the guts of the quotient; we simply invoked the torus's recursion
principle and paid its tolls using facts we had already proved about circles.
Large structures grow from small ones without ever reopening the foundations.

**Equivalence as the right notion of sameness.** When we said the torus *is*
two circles, we did not mean they are literally the same set of points. We
meant there is a lossless translation between them. In the cubical world this
notion of "sameness up to perfect translation" is the protagonist. It is the
shadow, at the level of plain sets, of one of the deepest principles in the
modern foundations of mathematics — the idea that equivalent structures may be
*identified*, treated as genuinely equal for all purposes. Our humble
torus-equals-two-circles theorem is a hands-on rehearsal of that principle.

## The road ahead

The constructions here are deliberately minimal — a one-dimensional gluing for
the circle and a two-dimensional gluing for the torus — and that minimality is
a feature. It exposes the skeleton of the subject so cleanly that the next
steps almost suggest themselves.

One can ask for a *dependent* recursion principle, which would let the target
of a function vary from point to point across the space — the difference
between painting a circle a single color and wrapping it in a ribbon whose
pattern changes as you go around. One can ask to *fill in* the square of the
torus with genuine two-dimensional cells, capturing not just the edges but the
surface they bound. One can try to compute, combinatorially, the famous
**fundamental group** that detects how loops wind around a space. And one can
seek a single, uniform "pushout" recipe that produces the circle, the torus,
spheres, and wedges all as instances of one master gluing construction.

Each of these is a natural extension of the same idea we have followed from the
very first piece of string: a space is what you get when you decide, carefully
and explicitly, which points to glue. Tie the ends of a string and you have a
circle. Glue the edges of a square and you have a doughnut. And a doughnut, it
turns out, is just two circles holding hands.

# A Set-Level Quotient Model of the Cubical Circle and Torus

**Author:** Aristotle
**Date:** 2026-06-24
**Domain:** Algebra (Type Theory / Cubical Foundations)

## Abstract

We develop a concrete, set-level ("0-truncated") model of two fundamental
higher inductive types — the circle $S^1$ and the torus $T^2$ — using only
quotient operations on the unit interval and the unit square. Following the
cubical philosophy in which spaces are generated by interval maps (*paths*) and
the gluing data is recorded by their *endpoints*, we define the circle as the
quotient of the unit interval that identifies its two endpoints, and the torus
as the quotient of the unit square that identifies opposite edges. For each
space we establish a non-dependent recursion principle with definitional
computation rules and a uniqueness theorem, mirroring the eliminators of a
higher inductive type. As the central application we prove that the torus is
equivalent to the product of two circles, $T^2 \simeq S^1 \times S^1$, by an
explicit pair of mutually inverse maps constructed entirely from the recursion
principles. The development is *acyclic* — the interval is defined first, then
the circle, then the torus — and uses only the standard quotient machinery,
keeping the logical footprint minimal. We discuss the constructions, give proof
sketches for all results, present algorithms realizing the eliminators, and
outline extensions to dependent eliminators, two-dimensional cell fillers,
combinatorial fundamental groups, and a uniform pushout recipe.

## 1. Introduction

Cubical type theory reorganizes the foundations of mathematics around a single
primitive: the **interval**. In this view a *path* in a space $X$ is a map from
the interval $\mathbb{I}$ into $X$; a *loop* is a path whose two endpoints
coincide; and higher-dimensional cells are maps out of higher cubes
$\mathbb{I}^n$. Complex spaces — the *higher inductive types* (HITs) such as
circles, spheres, tori, and suspensions — are presented by listing point
constructors together with path (and higher path) constructors that glue cube
boundaries.

The full cubical apparatus tracks an entire tower of higher coherences. In many
situations, however, one wants a *set-level* surrogate: an honest mathematical
object that reproduces the **point structure** and the **universal mapping
property** of a HIT without committing to its higher homotopical content. Such a
surrogate is valuable for three reasons. First, it is elementary: it requires
nothing beyond set-theoretic quotients. Second, it is *acyclic and auditable*:
every construction is a `Quot.lift`, and every gluing equation is a single use
of quotient soundness. Third, it isolates exactly which proof obligations a HIT
eliminator imposes — the "tolls" paid at each glued boundary — making the
recursion principles transparent.

This paper carries out that program for the two simplest interesting shapes
beyond the interval itself: the circle $S^1$ and the torus $T^2$. We model the
cubical interval by the closed real unit interval $\mathbb{I} = [0,1]$, with
endpoints $0$ and $1$. The circle is $\mathbb{I}$ with $0$ glued to $1$; the
torus is the square $\mathbb{I} \times \mathbb{I}$ with opposite edges glued.
For each we prove a recursion principle, computation rules, and a uniqueness
theorem. We then prove the main structural result, $T^2 \simeq S^1 \times S^1$,
with an explicit bi-directional equivalence.

### Contributions

1. A quotient definition of the cubical circle `Circle`, its base point, and
   its canonical loop, with the endpoint laws `loop_zero`, `loop_one`, and
   `loop_endpoints`.
2. A recursion principle `Circle.rec'` with definitional computation rules
   `rec_base` and `rec_loop`, a uniqueness theorem `rec_unique`, and
   surjectivity of the loop `loop_surjective`.
3. A quotient definition of the cubical torus `Torus` with edge-gluing laws
   `mk_horiz` and `mk_vert`, a recursion principle `Torus.rec'`, computation
   rule `rec_mk`, uniqueness theorem `rec_unique`, and surjectivity
   `mk_surjective`.
4. The equivalence `torusEquivCircles : Torus ≃ Circle × Circle`, built from
   the explicit maps `toCircles` and `ofCircles` together with the round-trip
   identities `left_inv` and `right_inv`.

## 2. Preliminaries: the cubical interval

We take the cubical interval to be the standard closed unit interval
$\mathbb{I} = \{ t \in \mathbb{R} : 0 \le t \le 1 \}$. Its two distinguished
points are the endpoints.

**Definition 2.1 (Endpoints).** Let $I_0 := 0 \in \mathbb{I}$ and
$I_1 := 1 \in \mathbb{I}$.

**Proposition 2.2 (`endpoints_ne`).** The endpoints are distinct: $I_0 \ne I_1$.

*Proof sketch.* The points $0$ and $1$ are distinct real numbers, hence
distinct as elements of the subtype $\mathbb{I}$; unfolding the definitions and
appealing to the order structure of $\mathbb{I}$ closes the goal. $\square$

The interval supplies all the raw material below. Every space we construct is a
quotient of a finite power of $\mathbb{I}$, and every map out of such a space is
produced by a quotient lift.

## 3. The cubical circle

**Definition 3.1 (Circle gluing relation).** Define a relation
$\mathrm{CircleRel}$ on $\mathbb{I}$ as the least relation with the single
generator
$$\mathrm{CircleRel}(0, 1).$$
That is, the only nontrivial identification is between the two endpoints.

**Definition 3.2 (Circle).** The **cubical circle** is the quotient
$$S^1 := \mathbb{I} \,/\, \mathrm{CircleRel} = \mathrm{Quot}\,(\mathrm{CircleRel}).$$

**Definition 3.3 (Base point and loop).**
The **base point** is $\mathrm{base} := [0]$, the class of the endpoint $0$.
The **loop** is the quotient projection
$$\mathrm{loop} : \mathbb{I} \to S^1, \qquad \mathrm{loop}(t) := [t].$$

The loop is the canonical interval map (path) into the circle. The defining
identification forces its endpoints to coincide.

**Proposition 3.4 (Endpoint laws).**
- (`loop_zero`) $\mathrm{loop}(0) = \mathrm{base}$.
- (`loop_one`) $\mathrm{loop}(1) = \mathrm{base}$.
- (`loop_endpoints`) $\mathrm{loop}(0) = \mathrm{loop}(1)$.

*Proof sketch.* The first is definitional: $\mathrm{base} = [0] =
\mathrm{loop}(0)$. The second follows from quotient soundness applied to the
generator $\mathrm{CircleRel}(0,1)$, giving $[0] = [1]$, i.e.
$\mathrm{loop}(1) = \mathrm{base}$. The third combines the two. $\square$

### 3.1 Recursion principle

The universal property of the quotient yields a non-dependent eliminator. Its
hypothesis is exactly the toll imposed by the gluing.

**Theorem 3.5 (Circle recursion, `Circle.rec'`).** Let $X$ be a type and
$f : \mathbb{I} \to X$ a map satisfying $f(0) = f(1)$. Then there is a map
$$\mathrm{rec}'(f, h) : S^1 \to X$$
characterized by $\mathrm{rec}'(f,h)([t]) = f(t)$.

*Proof sketch.* Apply $\mathrm{Quot.lift}$ to $f$. The required compatibility is
that $f$ respects $\mathrm{CircleRel}$; the unique generator $\mathrm{CircleRel}(0,1)$
demands $f(0) = f(1)$, which is the hypothesis $h$. $\square$

**Proposition 3.6 (Computation rules).** For $f$ and $h$ as above:
- (`rec_base`) $\mathrm{rec}'(f,h)(\mathrm{base}) = f(0)$;
- (`rec_loop`) $\mathrm{rec}'(f,h)(\mathrm{loop}(t)) = f(t)$ for all $t$.

*Proof sketch.* Both hold by definitional unfolding of $\mathrm{Quot.lift}$
(they are `rfl`). $\square$

**Theorem 3.7 (Uniqueness, `rec_unique`).** Let $f : \mathbb{I} \to X$ with
$f(0)=f(1)$, and let $g : S^1 \to X$ satisfy $g(\mathrm{loop}(t)) = f(t)$ for
all $t$. Then $g = \mathrm{rec}'(f,h)$.

*Proof sketch.* By function extensionality it suffices to check equality at
every point of $S^1$. By the quotient induction principle ($\mathrm{Quot.ind}$)
every point is of the form $[t] = \mathrm{loop}(t)$, where
$g(\mathrm{loop}(t)) = f(t) = \mathrm{rec}'(f,h)(\mathrm{loop}(t))$. $\square$

**Proposition 3.8 (Loop surjectivity, `loop_surjective`).** The loop is
surjective: every point of $S^1$ equals $\mathrm{loop}(t)$ for some $t$.

*Proof sketch.* Immediate from quotient induction: each class has a
representative $t$. $\square$

These results package $S^1$ with precisely the interface of a HIT: a point
constructor (`base`), a path constructor (`loop`) subject to the endpoint law,
a recursor with definitional computation rules, and a uniqueness statement that
says the recursor is the *only* map with the prescribed behavior on the loop.

## 4. The cubical torus

The torus is the two-dimensional analogue, obtained by gluing opposite edges of
the unit square $\mathbb{I} \times \mathbb{I}$.

**Definition 4.1 (Torus gluing relation).** Define a relation
$\mathrm{TorusRel}$ on $\mathbb{I} \times \mathbb{I}$ generated by two families:
$$\mathrm{TorusRel}\big((x,0),(x,1)\big) \quad \text{for all } x \quad
\text{(horizontal: bottom $\sim$ top)},$$
$$\mathrm{TorusRel}\big((0,y),(1,y)\big) \quad \text{for all } y \quad
\text{(vertical: left $\sim$ right)}.$$

**Definition 4.2 (Torus).** The **cubical torus** is the quotient
$$T^2 := (\mathbb{I} \times \mathbb{I}) \,/\, \mathrm{TorusRel}.$$
Its canonical square map is the projection $\mathrm{mk}(p) := [p]$.

**Proposition 4.3 (Edge laws).**
- (`mk_horiz`) $\mathrm{mk}(x,0) = \mathrm{mk}(x,1)$ for all $x$.
- (`mk_vert`) $\mathrm{mk}(0,y) = \mathrm{mk}(1,y)$ for all $y$.

*Proof sketch.* Each is a single application of quotient soundness to the
corresponding generator of $\mathrm{TorusRel}$. $\square$

### 4.1 Recursion principle

**Theorem 4.4 (Torus recursion, `Torus.rec'`).** Let $X$ be a type and
$f : \mathbb{I} \times \mathbb{I} \to X$ a map satisfying
$$f(x,0) = f(x,1) \ \text{for all } x \quad (h_h), \qquad
f(0,y) = f(1,y) \ \text{for all } y \quad (h_v).$$
Then there is a map $\mathrm{rec}'(f, h_h, h_v) : T^2 \to X$ with
$\mathrm{rec}'(f,h_h,h_v)([p]) = f(p)$.

*Proof sketch.* Apply $\mathrm{Quot.lift}$ to $f$, discharging the two families
of generators of $\mathrm{TorusRel}$ by $h_h$ (horizontal) and $h_v$
(vertical). $\square$

**Proposition 4.5 (Computation rule, `rec_mk`).**
$\mathrm{rec}'(f,h_h,h_v)(\mathrm{mk}(p)) = f(p)$ for all $p$.

*Proof sketch.* Definitional (`rfl`). $\square$

**Theorem 4.6 (Uniqueness, `rec_unique`).** If $g : T^2 \to X$ satisfies
$g(\mathrm{mk}(p)) = f(p)$ for all $p$, then $g = \mathrm{rec}'(f,h_h,h_v)$.

*Proof sketch.* Function extensionality plus quotient induction: every point of
$T^2$ is $[p] = \mathrm{mk}(p)$, where both sides equal $f(p)$. $\square$

**Proposition 4.7 (Surjectivity, `mk_surjective`).** The square map
$\mathrm{mk}$ is surjective.

*Proof sketch.* Quotient induction. $\square$

## 5. Main result: the torus is a product of two circles

We now show that the torus decomposes as a product of two circles. The
geometric intuition is that a point on the torus is determined by an
independent pair of angular coordinates — a longitude and a meridian — each of
which is a point on a circle.

**Definition 5.1 (Forward map, `toCircles`).** Define
$$\mathrm{toCircles} : T^2 \to S^1 \times S^1$$
by torus recursion applied to
$$f(x,y) := \big(\mathrm{loop}(x), \mathrm{loop}(y)\big).$$
The two tolls are paid as follows. The horizontal condition $f(x,0) = f(x,1)$
requires $\mathrm{loop}(0) = \mathrm{loop}(1)$ in the second coordinate, which
is `loop_endpoints`; the vertical condition $f(0,y) = f(1,y)$ requires the same
in the first coordinate. Hence $\mathrm{toCircles}(\mathrm{mk}(x,y)) =
(\mathrm{loop}(x), \mathrm{loop}(y))$.

**Definition 5.2 (Backward map, `ofCircles`).** Define
$$\mathrm{ofCircles} : S^1 \times S^1 \to T^2$$
by nested circle recursion. For a pair $(c_1, c_2)$, eliminate $c_1$ with the
family
$$x \mapsto \Big(\, \mathrm{rec}'\big(\, y \mapsto \mathrm{mk}(x,y),\ \texttt{mk\_horiz}(x)\,\big)\,\Big),$$
each inner recursor using the horizontal gluing `mk_horiz`$(x)$ as its toll;
the outer endpoint coherence is discharged by the vertical gluing `mk_vert`. On
representatives, $\mathrm{ofCircles}(\mathrm{loop}(x), \mathrm{loop}(y)) =
\mathrm{mk}(x,y)$.

**Theorem 5.3 (Left inverse, `left_inv`).** For every $t \in T^2$,
$$\mathrm{ofCircles}(\mathrm{toCircles}(t)) = t.$$

*Proof sketch.* By quotient induction it suffices to treat $t = \mathrm{mk}(p)$
with $p = (x,y)$. Then $\mathrm{toCircles}(\mathrm{mk}(x,y)) =
(\mathrm{loop}(x), \mathrm{loop}(y))$ and
$\mathrm{ofCircles}(\mathrm{loop}(x), \mathrm{loop}(y)) = \mathrm{mk}(x,y)$ by
the computation rules; both reductions are definitional, so the composite is
the identity (`rfl`). $\square$

**Theorem 5.4 (Right inverse, `right_inv`).** For every
$(c_1,c_2) \in S^1 \times S^1$,
$$\mathrm{toCircles}(\mathrm{ofCircles}(c_1,c_2)) = (c_1,c_2).$$

*Proof sketch.* Apply quotient induction to each coordinate, reducing $c_1 =
\mathrm{loop}(x)$ and $c_2 = \mathrm{loop}(y)$. Then $\mathrm{ofCircles}$
produces $\mathrm{mk}(x,y)$ and $\mathrm{toCircles}$ returns
$(\mathrm{loop}(x), \mathrm{loop}(y)) = (c_1,c_2)$ by the computation rules.
$\square$

**Theorem 5.5 (`torusEquivCircles`).** There is an equivalence
$$T^2 \;\simeq\; S^1 \times S^1$$
with underlying functions $\mathrm{toCircles}$ and $\mathrm{ofCircles}$.

*Proof sketch.* The data of an equivalence is a pair of maps together with both
round-trip identities; these are supplied by `toCircles`, `ofCircles`,
`left_inv`, and `right_inv`. $\square$

This theorem is the set-level shadow of the homotopy-theoretic fact that the
torus is the product $S^1 \times S^1$. Notably, the entire proof never reopens
the quotient definitions: it operates purely through the recursion principles
and the endpoint/edge gluing laws, demonstrating that those interfaces are
sufficient to reason about the constructed spaces.

## 6. Worked examples

To make the recursion principles concrete, we record three illustrative maps
produced by the eliminators. None of them require any topology; each is a single
quotient lift gated by an endpoint or edge toll.

**Example 6.1 (A real-valued function on the circle).** Let $X = \mathbb{R}$ and
define $f(t) = \cos(2\pi t)$ on $\mathbb{I}$. Since $\cos(0) = \cos(2\pi) = 1$,
the toll $f(0) = f(1)$ holds, so by Theorem 3.5 there is a well-defined map
$\hat f := \mathrm{rec}'(f, h) : S^1 \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\hat f(\mathrm{loop}(t))
= \cos(2\pi t)$ and $\hat f(\mathrm{base}) = 1$. This is the prototypical example
of a function that "sees" the circle as a periodic domain: any periodic profile
of period $1$ on the interval descends to the circle, and conversely (by
Theorem 3.7) any map out of the circle arises this way from a unique periodic
profile. A non-periodic profile such as $g(t) = t$ fails the toll, $g(0) = 0 \ne
1 = g(1)$, and correctly does *not* descend — there is no function on the circle
that increases monotonically all the way around.

**Example 6.2 (A height function on the torus).** Let $X = \mathbb{R}$ and define
$f(x,y) = \sin(2\pi x) + \sin(2\pi y)$ on the square. Both edge tolls hold:
$f(x,0) = \sin(2\pi x) = f(x,1)$ and $f(0,y) = \sin(2\pi y) = f(1,y)$. Hence by
Theorem 4.4 there is a map $\hat f : T^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$\hat f(\mathrm{mk}(x,y)) = \sin(2\pi x) + \sin(2\pi y)$. This is a doubly
periodic "height" on the torus, the kind of function one integrates in Fourier
analysis on $T^2$; the recursion principle is precisely the statement that
doubly periodic functions on the square are the same as functions on the torus.

**Example 6.3 (The identity via the equivalence).** Composing $\mathrm{ofCircles}$
after $\mathrm{toCircles}$ produces the identity on $T^2$ (Theorem 5.3). Tracing a
representative $(x,y)$ through the two maps gives
$\mathrm{mk}(x,y) \mapsto (\mathrm{loop}(x),\mathrm{loop}(y)) \mapsto
\mathrm{mk}(x,y)$, and each arrow is a definitional computation rule. This is the
sense in which the equivalence is "transparent": it introduces no genuine
computation, only a relabelling of coordinates.

## 7. Algorithms

The recursion principles are *constructive recipes* for defining maps. We make
them explicit.

**Algorithm A (Circle eliminator).** Input: a target $X$, a map
$f : \mathbb{I} \to X$, and a proof $h : f(0) = f(1)$. Output: a map
$S^1 \to X$. The procedure lifts $f$ along the quotient projection; the proof
$h$ is precisely the obligation that $f$ be constant on the single gluing pair
$(0,1)$. On any input $[t]$ it returns $f(t)$ in one step.

**Algorithm B (Torus eliminator).** Input: a target $X$, a map
$f : \mathbb{I}\times\mathbb{I} \to X$, and proofs $h_h, h_v$ of edge agreement.
Output: a map $T^2 \to X$. The procedure lifts $f$, discharging the two
generator families using $h_h$ and $h_v$. On any input $[p]$ it returns $f(p)$.

**Algorithm C (Torus $\leftrightarrow$ circles translation).** Compose the two
eliminators. Forward: lift $(x,y) \mapsto (\mathrm{loop}\,x, \mathrm{loop}\,y)$.
Backward: nest two circle eliminators, the inner over the second coordinate
with toll `mk_horiz`, the outer over the first with toll `mk_vert`. Both
round-trips reduce to identities by the computation rules.

These algorithms run in constant time on representatives, because each lift
reduces definitionally: the cost of the abstraction is entirely in the *proof
obligations* (the tolls), not in any runtime computation.

## 8. Applications and discussion

**A blueprint for HIT eliminators.** The development demonstrates, at the
gentlest possible scale, the exact pattern by which higher inductive types are
used: construct by quotient, compute on generators, conclude by uniqueness. The
tolls $f(0)=f(1)$ (circle) and the edge agreements (torus) are the set-level
manifestations of the *path constructors* of the corresponding HITs.

**Equivalence as identification.** Theorem 5.5 is a concrete rehearsal of the
univalence principle's spirit: two differently presented objects (a quotient of
a square versus a product of two quotients of an interval) are shown to be
interchangeable via a lossless translation. While the present model is
0-truncated and therefore does not carry univalence's higher content, it makes
the *shape* of such reasoning fully explicit and machine-checkable.

**Minimal logical footprint.** Every result rests only on quotients
($\mathrm{Quot}$, $\mathrm{Quot.lift}$, $\mathrm{Quot.sound}$,
$\mathrm{Quot.ind}$) and function extensionality. The build is acyclic:
interval $\Rightarrow$ circle $\Rightarrow$ torus, with no forward references.

**Limitations.** Because the model is set-level, it deliberately discards higher
homotopical information. The loop is non-degenerate *as data*, but the model has
no native path-between-paths, so it cannot by itself detect, e.g., that the
fundamental group of $S^1$ is $\mathbb{Z}$. The recursion principles provided
are non-dependent; a dependent eliminator requires making endpoint transport
explicit (see §9).

## 9. Future directions

The following directions extend the concrete quotient model of basic cubical
shapes.

**8.1 A dependent eliminator for the quotient circle.** The present development
supplies only the non-dependent recursor `Circle.rec'`, covering maps
$S^1 \to X$. The natural next step is a dependent eliminator that, given a
motive $P : S^1 \to \mathrm{Type}$, a point $b : P(\mathrm{base})$, and a loop
datum identifying the two transported endpoints, produces a section of $P$. The
key insight is that the dependent case forces the endpoint transport to be
*explicit*: in a set-theoretic model there is no native transport, so the user
must supply the identification $b = b$ along the loop as data, exactly as a HIT
eliminator demands. This can be prototyped against the known-good non-dependent
recursor (whose computation rule is `rfl`), isolating the extra coherence
obligations cleanly.

**8.2 Filling the torus square with explicit 2-cells.** The torus carries a
meridian and a longitude that are independent by `rfl`, but the model has no
native path-between-paths, so the commuting square a genuine $T^2$ requires is
currently absent. The key insight is that, in a quotient model, a 2-cell is
itself a quotient of the unit square by a boundary-gluing relation, so the same
explicit-relation recipe that built $S^1$ should build the filler directly,
reusing the `Quot.sound` pattern and validating incrementally.

**8.3 Computing a set-theoretic fundamental group.** It is unclear how much
homotopical content survives when continuity is dropped: the loop exists and is
non-degenerate as data, but without topology the usual winding-number argument
is unavailable. The key insight is that in this discrete model the "fundamental
group" should be reconstructed combinatorially as the free structure generated
by the loop modulo the explicitly imposed endpoint relations, turning a
topological invariant into a purely algebraic quotient, and testing whether the
algebraic reconstruction is faithful or collapses to the trivial group.

**8.4 A uniform pushout recipe for explicit gluing.** The circle arises by
gluing the two endpoints of an interval, and many further shapes (suspensions,
spheres, wedges) arise by analogous gluings. The key insight is that all of
these are instances of a single quotient-of-a-coproduct pattern, so a generic
`Pushout` construction parameterized by an explicit span relation would subsume
the circle relation as one special case.

## 10. Conclusion

We have given a compact, fully explicit, set-level model of the cubical circle
and torus using only quotients of the interval and the square. Each space comes
with a recursion principle, definitional computation rules, and a uniqueness
theorem, and we proved the structural identity $T^2 \simeq S^1 \times S^1$ via
an explicit equivalence. The development distills the cubical creed — *spaces
are made by gluing the boundaries of cubes* — into its most elementary,
auditable form, and provides a clean baseline from which dependent eliminators,
higher cells, combinatorial invariants, and uniform pushouts can be built.

We develop a concrete, set-level (``$0$-truncated'') model of two fundamental
higher inductive types --- the circle $\Sone$ and the torus $\Ttwo$ --- using
only quotient operations on the unit interval and the unit square. Following the
cubical philosophy in which spaces are generated by interval maps (\emph{paths})
and the gluing data is recorded by their \emph{endpoints}, we define the circle
as the quotient of the unit interval that identifies its two endpoints, and the
torus as the quotient of the unit square that identifies opposite edges. For
each space we establish a non-dependent recursion principle with definitional
computation rules and a uniqueness theorem, mirroring the eliminators of a
higher inductive type. As the central application we prove that the torus is
equivalent to the product of two circles, $\Ttwo \simeq \Sone \times \Sone$, by
an explicit pair of mutually inverse maps constructed entirely from the
recursion principles. The development is \emph{acyclic} --- interval, then
circle, then torus --- and uses only standard quotient machinery, keeping the
logical footprint minimal. We discuss the constructions, give proof sketches for
all results, present algorithms realizing the eliminators, and outline
extensions to dependent eliminators, two-dimensional cell fillers, combinatorial
fundamental groups, and a uniform pushout recipe.

\section{Introduction}

Cubical type theory reorganizes the foundations of mathematics around a single
primitive: the \textbf{interval}. In this view a \emph{path} in a space $X$ is a
map from the interval $\I$ into $X$; a \emph{loop} is a path whose two endpoints
coincide; and higher-dimensional cells are maps out of higher cubes $\I^n$.
Complex spaces --- the \emph{higher inductive types} (HITs) such as circles,
spheres, tori, and suspensions --- are presented by listing point constructors
together with path (and higher path) constructors that glue cube boundaries.

The full cubical apparatus tracks an entire tower of higher coherences. In many
situations, however, one wants a \emph{set-level} surrogate: an honest
mathematical object that reproduces the \textbf{point structure} and the
\textbf{universal mapping property} of a HIT without committing to its higher
homotopical content. Such a surrogate is elementary (requiring nothing beyond
set-theoretic quotients), acyclic and auditable (every construction is a quotient
lift and every gluing equation a single use of quotient soundness), and it
isolates exactly which proof obligations a HIT eliminator imposes --- the
``tolls'' paid at each glued boundary.

This paper carries out that program for the two simplest interesting shapes
beyond the interval itself: the circle $\Sone$ and the torus $\Ttwo$. We model
the cubical interval by the closed real unit interval $\I = [0,1]$, with
endpoints $0$ and $1$. The circle is $\I$ with $0$ glued to $1$; the torus is
the square $\I \times \I$ with opposite edges glued. For each we prove a
recursion principle, computation rules, and a uniqueness theorem. We then prove
the main structural result $\Ttwo \simeq \Sone \times \Sone$ with an explicit
bi-directional equivalence.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A quotient definition of the cubical circle, its base point, and its
  canonical loop, with the endpoint laws \texttt{loop\_zero},
  \texttt{loop\_one}, \texttt{loop\_endpoints}.
  \item A recursion principle \texttt{Circle.rec'} with definitional computation
  rules \texttt{rec\_base}, \texttt{rec\_loop}, a uniqueness theorem
  \texttt{rec\_unique}, and loop surjectivity \texttt{loop\_surjective}.
  \item A quotient definition of the cubical torus with edge-gluing laws
  \texttt{mk\_horiz}, \texttt{mk\_vert}, a recursion principle
  \texttt{Torus.rec'}, computation rule \texttt{rec\_mk}, uniqueness
  \texttt{rec\_unique}, and surjectivity \texttt{mk\_surjective}.
  \item The equivalence \texttt{torusEquivCircles}:
  $\Ttwo \simeq \Sone \times \Sone$, built from \texttt{toCircles},
  \texttt{ofCircles} and the round-trip identities \texttt{left\_inv},
  \texttt{right\_inv}.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Preliminaries: the cubical interval}

We take the cubical interval to be the standard closed unit interval
$\I = \{ t \in \mathbb{R} : 0 \le t \le 1 \}$, with two distinguished endpoints.

\begin{definition}[Endpoints]
Let $I_0 := 0 \in \I$ and $I_1 := 1 \in \I$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[\texttt{endpoints\_ne}]
The endpoints are distinct: $I_0 \ne I_1$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The reals $0$ and $1$ are distinct, hence distinct as elements of the subtype
$\I$; unfolding the definitions and appealing to the order structure closes the
goal.
\end{proof}

Every space below is a quotient of a finite power of $\I$, and every map out of
such a space is produced by a quotient lift.

\section{The cubical circle}

\begin{definition}[Circle gluing relation]
Define $\mathrm{CircleRel}$ on $\I$ as the least relation with the single
generator $\mathrm{CircleRel}(0,1)$: the only nontrivial identification is
between the two endpoints.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Circle]
The \textbf{cubical circle} is the quotient
$\Sone := \I / \mathrm{CircleRel} = \mathrm{Quot}\,(\mathrm{CircleRel})$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Base point and loop]
The \textbf{base point} is $\base := [0]$, the class of the endpoint $0$. The
\textbf{loop} is the quotient projection $\loopmap : \I \to \Sone$,
$\loopmap(t) := [t]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Endpoint laws]
$\loopmap(0) = \base$ (\texttt{loop\_zero}); $\loopmap(1) = \base$
(\texttt{loop\_one}); and $\loopmap(0) = \loopmap(1)$ (\texttt{loop\_endpoints}).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The first is definitional. The second follows from quotient soundness applied to
$\mathrm{CircleRel}(0,1)$, giving $[0]=[1]$. The third combines them.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Recursion principle}

\begin{theorem}[Circle recursion, \texttt{Circle.rec'}]
Let $X$ be a type and $f : \I \to X$ with $f(0)=f(1)$. Then there is a map
$\rec(f,h) : \Sone \to X$ characterized by $\rec(f,h)([t]) = f(t)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply $\mathrm{Quot.lift}$ to $f$; the compatibility obligation for the unique
generator $\mathrm{CircleRel}(0,1)$ is exactly $f(0)=f(1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Computation rules]
$\rec(f,h)(\base) = f(0)$ (\texttt{rec\_base}) and
$\rec(f,h)(\loopmap(t)) = f(t)$ (\texttt{rec\_loop}); both hold definitionally.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness, \texttt{rec\_unique}]
If $g : \Sone \to X$ satisfies $g(\loopmap(t)) = f(t)$ for all $t$, then
$g = \rec(f,h)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By function extensionality and quotient induction, every point is
$[t]=\loopmap(t)$, where both sides equal $f(t)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Loop surjectivity, \texttt{loop\_surjective}]
Every point of $\Sone$ equals $\loopmap(t)$ for some $t$.
\end{proposition}

\section{The cubical torus}

\begin{definition}[Torus gluing relation]
Define $\mathrm{TorusRel}$ on $\I \times \I$ generated by
$\mathrm{TorusRel}((x,0),(x,1))$ for all $x$ (horizontal: bottom $\sim$ top) and
$\mathrm{TorusRel}((0,y),(1,y))$ for all $y$ (vertical: left $\sim$ right).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Torus]
The \textbf{cubical torus} is $\Ttwo := (\I \times \I)/\mathrm{TorusRel}$, with
canonical square map $\mk(p) := [p]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Edge laws]
$\mk(x,0)=\mk(x,1)$ (\texttt{mk\_horiz}) and $\mk(0,y)=\mk(1,y)$
(\texttt{mk\_vert}), each by quotient soundness on the corresponding generator.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Torus recursion, \texttt{Torus.rec'}]
Let $f : \I \times \I \to X$ satisfy $f(x,0)=f(x,1)$ for all $x$ ($h_h$) and
$f(0,y)=f(1,y)$ for all $y$ ($h_v$). Then there is a map
$\rec(f,h_h,h_v) : \Ttwo \to X$ with $\rec(f,h_h,h_v)([p]) = f(p)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Apply $\mathrm{Quot.lift}$ to $f$, discharging the two generator families by
$h_h$ and $h_v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Computation rule, \texttt{rec\_mk}]
$\rec(f,h_h,h_v)(\mk(p)) = f(p)$, definitionally.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness, \texttt{rec\_unique}]
If $g : \Ttwo \to X$ satisfies $g(\mk(p)) = f(p)$ for all $p$, then
$g = \rec(f,h_h,h_v)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[Surjectivity, \texttt{mk\_surjective}]
The square map $\mk$ is surjective.
\end{proposition}

\section{Main result: the torus is a product of two circles}

The geometric intuition is that a point on the torus is an independent pair of
angular coordinates --- a longitude and a meridian --- each a point on a circle.

\begin{definition}[Forward map, \texttt{toCircles}]
Define $\toCircles : \Ttwo \to \Sone \times \Sone$ by torus recursion applied to
$f(x,y) := (\loopmap(x), \loopmap(y))$. The horizontal toll requires
$\loopmap(0)=\loopmap(1)$ in the second coordinate (\texttt{loop\_endpoints});
the vertical toll requires the same in the first. Hence
$\toCircles(\mk(x,y)) = (\loopmap(x),\loopmap(y))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Backward map, \texttt{ofCircles}]
Define $\ofCircles : \Sone \times \Sone \to \Ttwo$ by nested circle recursion.
For $(c_1,c_2)$, eliminate $c_1$ with the family
$x \mapsto \rec(\,y \mapsto \mk(x,y),\ \texttt{mk\_horiz}(x)\,)$, each inner
recursor using \texttt{mk\_horiz}$(x)$ as toll; the outer coherence is
discharged by \texttt{mk\_vert}. On representatives,
$\ofCircles(\loopmap(x),\loopmap(y)) = \mk(x,y)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Left inverse, \texttt{left\_inv}]
For every $t \in \Ttwo$, $\ofCircles(\toCircles(t)) = t$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By quotient induction, treat $t = \mk(x,y)$. Then $\toCircles(\mk(x,y)) =
(\loopmap(x),\loopmap(y))$ and $\ofCircles(\loopmap(x),\loopmap(y)) = \mk(x,y)$
by the computation rules; the composite is the identity definitionally.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Right inverse, \texttt{right\_inv}]
For every $(c_1,c_2) \in \Sone \times \Sone$,
$\toCircles(\ofCircles(c_1,c_2)) = (c_1,c_2)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Quotient induction on each coordinate reduces to $c_1=\loopmap(x)$,
$c_2=\loopmap(y)$; then $\ofCircles$ yields $\mk(x,y)$ and $\toCircles$ returns
$(\loopmap(x),\loopmap(y))$ by the computation rules.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{torusEquivCircles}]
There is an equivalence $\Ttwo \simeq \Sone \times \Sone$ with underlying
functions $\toCircles$ and $\ofCircles$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
An equivalence is a pair of maps with both round-trip identities; these are
\texttt{toCircles}, \texttt{ofCircles}, \texttt{left\_inv}, \texttt{right\_inv}.
\end{proof}

This is the set-level shadow of the homotopy-theoretic fact that the torus is the
product $\Sone \times \Sone$. The proof never reopens the quotient definitions:
it works purely through the recursion principles and gluing laws.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Algorithm A (Circle eliminator).} Input: target $X$, map
$f : \I \to X$, proof $h : f(0)=f(1)$. Lift $f$ along the quotient projection;
$h$ is the obligation that $f$ be constant on the gluing pair $(0,1)$. On $[t]$
return $f(t)$.

\paragraph{Algorithm B (Torus eliminator).} Input: target $X$, map
$f : \I\times\I \to X$, proofs $h_h, h_v$ of edge agreement. Lift $f$,
discharging the two generator families. On $[p]$ return $f(p)$.

\paragraph{Algorithm C (Torus $\leftrightarrow$ circles).} Forward: lift
$(x,y) \mapsto (\loopmap\,x, \loopmap\,y)$. Backward: nest two circle
eliminators, inner over the second coordinate (toll \texttt{mk\_horiz}), outer
over the first (toll \texttt{mk\_vert}). Both round-trips reduce to identities.

All lifts reduce definitionally; the cost is in the proof obligations, not in
runtime computation.

\section{Applications and discussion}

The development demonstrates, at the gentlest scale, the pattern by which HITs
are used: construct by quotient, compute on generators, conclude by uniqueness.
The tolls $f(0)=f(1)$ (circle) and edge agreements (torus) are the set-level
manifestations of the path constructors. The equivalence theorem is a concrete
rehearsal of the univalence principle's spirit --- two differently presented
objects shown interchangeable via a lossless translation --- though the model is
$0$-truncated and does not carry univalence's higher content. Every result rests
only on quotients ($\mathrm{Quot}$, $\mathrm{Quot.lift}$, $\mathrm{Quot.sound}$,
$\mathrm{Quot.ind}$) and function extensionality, with an acyclic build.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Being set-level, the model discards higher homotopical
information: the loop is non-degenerate as data but there is no native
path-between-paths, so it cannot itself detect $\pi_1(\Sone)=\mathbb{Z}$. The
recursion principles are non-dependent.

\section{Future directions}

\paragraph{Dependent eliminator for the quotient circle.} Beyond the
non-dependent \texttt{Circle.rec'}, a dependent eliminator takes a motive
$P : \Sone \to \mathrm{Type}$, a point $b : P(\base)$, and a loop datum
identifying the two transported endpoints, producing a section of $P$. The
dependent case forces explicit endpoint transport: with no native transport, the
identification $b=b$ along the loop must be supplied as data, exactly as a HIT
eliminator demands.

\paragraph{Filling the torus square with explicit 2-cells.} The meridian and
longitude are independent by \texttt{rfl}, but the model lacks
path-between-paths, so the commuting square a genuine $\Ttwo$ requires is absent.
A $2$-cell is itself a quotient of the unit square by a boundary-gluing relation,
so the same explicit-relation recipe should build the filler, reusing the
\texttt{Quot.sound} pattern incrementally.

\paragraph{Computing a set-theoretic fundamental group.} Without topology the
winding-number argument is unavailable. The ``fundamental group'' should be
reconstructed combinatorially as the free structure generated by the loop modulo
the imposed endpoint relations, testing whether this reconstruction is faithful
or collapses to the trivial group.

\paragraph{A uniform pushout recipe for explicit gluing.} The circle, torus,
suspensions, spheres, and wedges are instances of one
quotient-of-a-coproduct pattern, so a generic pushout construction parameterized
by an explicit span relation would subsume the circle relation as a special case.

\section{Conclusion}

We gave a compact, fully explicit, set-level model of the cubical circle and
torus using only quotients of the interval and square. Each space comes with a
recursion principle, definitional computation rules, and a uniqueness theorem,
and we proved $\Ttwo \simeq \Sone \times \Sone$ via an explicit equivalence. The
development distills the cubical creed --- spaces are made by gluing boundaries
of cubes --- into its most elementary, auditable form, and gives a clean
baseline for dependent eliminators, higher cells, combinatorial invariants, and
uniform pushouts.

"""
Numerical / computational demonstration of the set-level quotient model of the
cubical circle (S^1) and torus (T^2).

This script mirrors the Lean development:

  * The cubical interval is modeled by floats in [0, 1].
  * The circle S^1 is the interval with endpoints 0 ~ 1 glued.
  * The torus T^2 is the square [0,1]^2 with opposite edges glued.
  * Each space carries a recursion principle (eliminator) that requires the
    "toll" equations enforced by the gluing.
  * We exhibit the equivalence T^2 ~= S^1 x S^1 via explicit mutually inverse
    maps `to_circles` and `of_circles`, and verify the round-trip identities
    numerically.

Everything is self-contained and uses only the standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, Tuple, TypeVar

X = TypeVar("X")

EPS = 1e-12


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical interval and its endpoints
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def in_interval(t: float) -> bool:
    """Membership test for the unit interval I = [0, 1]."""
    return -EPS <= t <= 1.0 + EPS


I0: float = 0.0  # the 0 endpoint
I1: float = 1.0  # the 1 endpoint


def endpoints_ne() -> bool:
    """Proposition `endpoints_ne`: the two endpoints are distinct."""
    return abs(I0 - I1) > EPS


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical circle  S^1 = I / (0 ~ 1)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# A point of S^1 is represented by a canonical interval representative in [0, 1),
# i.e. we normalize the endpoint 1 down to 0, since loop(1) = loop(0) = base.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Circle:
    """A point of the cubical circle, stored as a canonical representative."""
    rep: float  # canonical representative in [0, 1)


def loop(t: float) -> Circle:
    """The canonical interval map (loop) into the circle.

    Sends every interval point t to its class; the endpoint 1 is identified
    with 0 (the gluing 0 ~ 1), realizing loop_zero / loop_one / loop_endpoints.
    """
    assert in_interval(t)
    if abs(t - 1.0) <= EPS:
        return Circle(0.0)
    return Circle(t)


BASE: Circle = loop(0.0)  # the base point = common image of the two endpoints


def circle_rec(f: Callable[[float], X], h: bool) -> Callable[[Circle], X]:
    """Recursion principle `Circle.rec'`.

    Given an interval map f : I -> X whose endpoints agree (the toll
    h : f(0) == f(1)), induces a map S^1 -> X with computation rule
    rec(loop t) = f t  and  rec(base) = f 0.
    """
    if not h:
        raise ValueError("circle_rec: endpoint toll f(0) = f(1) not satisfied")

    def induced(c: Circle) -> X:
        return f(c.rep)

    return induced


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical torus  T^2 = (I x I) / (opposite edges glued)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Torus:
    """A point of the cubical torus, stored as a canonical square representative."""
    x: float  # canonical first coordinate in [0, 1)
    y: float  # canonical second coordinate in [0, 1)


def torus_mk(p: Tuple[float, float]) -> Torus:
    """The canonical square map into the torus.

    Glues bottom~top  ((x,0)~(x,1))  and  left~right  ((0,y)~(1,y))  by
    normalizing each coordinate's endpoint 1 down to 0.
    """
    x, y = p
    assert in_interval(x) and in_interval(y)
    nx = 0.0 if abs(x - 1.0) <= EPS else x
    ny = 0.0 if abs(y - 1.0) <= EPS else y
    return Torus(nx, ny)


def torus_rec(
    f: Callable[[Tuple[float, float]], X],
    hh: bool,
    hv: bool,
) -> Callable[[Torus], X]:
    """Recursion principle `Torus.rec'`.

    Given a square map f together with the two edge tolls
    hh : f(x,0) == f(x,1)  and  hv : f(0,y) == f(1,y),
    induces a map T^2 -> X with computation rule rec(mk p) = f p.
    """
    if not (hh and hv):
        raise ValueError("torus_rec: edge tolls not satisfied")

    def induced(t: Torus) -> X:
        return f((t.x, t.y))

    return induced


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The equivalence  T^2 ~= S^1 x S^1
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def to_circles(t: Torus) -> Tuple[Circle, Circle]:
    """`toCircles`: a torus point goes to its (longitude, meridian) pair."""
    return (loop(t.x), loop(t.y))


def of_circles(pair: Tuple[Circle, Circle]) -> Torus:
    """`ofCircles`: a pair of circle points reassembles a torus point."""
    c1, c2 = pair
    return torus_mk((c1.rep, c2.rep))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

    print("=== Circle: endpoint gluing (loop_zero / loop_one / loop_endpoints) ===")
    print(f"  endpoints_ne (0 != 1 in I)?  {endpoints_ne()}")
    print(f"  loop(0) == base ?            {loop(0.0) == BASE}")
    print(f"  loop(1) == base ?            {loop(1.0) == BASE}")
    print(f"  loop(0) == loop(1) ?         {loop(0.0) == loop(1.0)}")
    print()


def demo_circle_rec() -> None:
    print("=== Circle recursion principle (rec_base / rec_loop) ===")
    # f(t) = cos(2 pi t) has f(0) = f(1) = 1, so it descends to the circle.
    import math
    f = lambda t: round(math.cos(2 * math.pi * t), 10)
    toll = abs(f(0.0) - f(1.0)) <= 1e-9
    g = circle_rec(f, toll)
    for t in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75):
        print(f"  g(loop({t})) = f({t}) = {g(loop(t))}")
    print(f"  g(base) = f(0) = {g(BASE)}")
    print()

    print("=== Torus: opposite-edge gluing (mk_horiz / mk_vert) ===")
    samples = [0.0, 0.3, 0.7]
    horiz = all(torus_mk((x, 0.0)) == torus_mk((x, 1.0)) for x in samples)
    vert = all(torus_mk((0.0, y)) == torus_mk((1.0, y)) for y in samples)
    print(f"  mk(x,0) == mk(x,1) for all sampled x ?  {horiz}")
    print(f"  mk(0,y) == mk(1,y) for all sampled y ?  {vert}")
    print()

    torus_pts = [torus_mk((x, y))
                 for x in (0.0, 0.2, 0.6)
                 for y in (0.0, 0.4, 0.9)]
    left_ok = all(of_circles(to_circles(t)) == t for t in torus_pts)
    print(f"  ofCircles(toCircles(t)) == t  for all sampled t ?  {left_ok}")

    circle_pairs = [(loop(x), loop(y))
                    for x in (0.0, 0.2, 0.6)
                    for y in (0.0, 0.4, 0.9)]

    print(f"  toCircles(ofCircles(p)) == p  for all sampled p ?  {right_ok}")
    print()

    demo_circle_rec()
    demo_torus_edges()
    demo_equivalence()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")

from typing import Callable, Tuple, TypeVar

X = TypeVar("X")

EPS = 1e-12


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical interval and its endpoints
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def in_interval(t: float) -> bool:
    """Membership test for the unit interval I = [0, 1]."""
    return -EPS <= t <= 1.0 + EPS


I0: float = 0.0  # the 0 endpoint
I1: float = 1.0  # the 1 endpoint


def endpoints_ne() -> bool:
    """Proposition `endpoints_ne`: the two endpoints are distinct."""
    return abs(I0 - I1) > EPS


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical circle  S^1 = I / (0 ~ 1)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# A point of S^1 is represented by a canonical interval representative in [0, 1),
# i.e. we normalize the endpoint 1 down to 0, since loop(1) = loop(0) = base.

class Circle:
    """A point of the cubical circle, stored as a canonical representative."""
    rep: float  # canonical representative in [0, 1)


def loop(t: float) -> Circle:
    """The canonical interval map (loop) into the circle.

    Sends every interval point t to its class; the endpoint 1 is identified
    with 0 (the gluing 0 ~ 1), realizing loop_zero / loop_one / loop_endpoints.
    """
    assert in_interval(t)
    if abs(t - 1.0) <= EPS:
        return Circle(0.0)
    return Circle(t)


BASE: Circle = loop(0.0)  # the base point = common image of the two endpoints

    """Recursion principle `Circle.rec'`.

    if not h:

        return f(c.rep)

    x: float  # canonical first coordinate in [0, 1)
    y: float  # canonical second coordinate in [0, 1)

    hv: bool,

    induces a map T^2 -> X with computation rule rec(mk p) = f p.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Cubical Semantics: the cubical circle and torus

This file gives a set-level ("0-truncated") surrogate for two basic higher inductive
types — the circle `S¹` and the torus `T²` — built by *quotient operations* on the
unit interval, following the cubical philosophy in which spaces are generated by
*interval maps* (paths) and the gluing data is recorded by their *endpoints*.

The constructions are purely algorithmic: every map out of a generated space is
produced by a `Quot.lift` recursor, and the gluing relations are exactly the
endpoint identifications of the interval.  The build is *acyclic*: the cubical
interval is defined first, the circle is the quotient of the interval by gluing its
two endpoints, and the torus is the quotient of the square by gluing opposite edges.
No definition depends on a later one.

## Main definitions

- `CubicalSemantics.I0`, `CubicalSemantics.I1` — the two endpoints of the cubical
  interval (Mathlib's `unitInterval`).
- `CubicalSemantics.Circle` — the cubical circle, `unitInterval` quotiented by the
  relation gluing `0` to `1`.
- `CubicalSemantics.Circle.loop` — the canonical interval map (loop) into the circle.
- `CubicalSemantics.Circle.rec'` — the recursion principle: an interval map whose two
  endpoints agree induces a map out of the circle.
- `CubicalSemantics.Torus` — the cubical torus, the square `unitInterval × unitInterval`
  quotiented by gluing opposite edges.
- `CubicalSemantics.Torus.rec'` — the recursion principle for the torus.
- `CubicalSemantics.torusEquivCircles` — the torus is `Circle × Circle`.

## Main results

- `Circle.loop_zero`, `Circle.loop_one` — the loop sends both endpoints to the base
  point (endpoint behaviour).
- `Circle.rec_base`, `Circle.rec_loop`, `Circle.rec_unique` — computation and
  uniqueness rules for the circle recursor.
- `Torus.rec_mk`, `Torus.rec_unique` — computation and uniqueness rules for the torus
  recursor.
- `torusEquivCircles` — `Torus ≃ Circle × Circle`.
-/

open unitInterval

namespace CubicalSemantics

/-! ## The cubical interval

We use Mathlib's `unitInterval` as the cubical interval.  Its two endpoints are the
points `0` and `1`; everything below is generated from these. -/

/-- The `0` endpoint of the cubical interval. -/
def I0 : unitInterval := 0

/-- The `1` endpoint of the cubical interval. -/
def I1 : unitInterval := 1

/-- The two endpoints of the cubical interval are distinct. -/
theorem endpoints_ne : I0 ≠ I1 := by
  simp [I0, I1, unitInterval]

/-! ## The cubical circle

The circle is the quotient of the interval that glues its two endpoints together. -/

/-- The gluing relation for the circle: identify the two endpoints `0` and `1`. -/
inductive CircleRel : unitInterval → unitInterval → Prop where
  | glue : CircleRel 0 1

/-- The cubical circle: the unit interval with its endpoints glued. -/
def Circle : Type := Quot CircleRel

namespace Circle

/-- The base point of the circle, the common image of the two endpoints. -/
def base : Circle := Quot.mk _ 0

/-- The canonical interval map (loop) into the circle. -/
def loop (t : unitInterval) : Circle := Quot.mk _ t

/-- Endpoint behaviour: the loop sends the `0` endpoint to the base point. -/
theorem loop_zero : loop 0 = base := rfl

/-- Endpoint behaviour: the loop sends the `1` endpoint to the base point. -/
theorem loop_one : loop 1 = base := (Quot.sound CircleRel.glue).symm

/-- The loop is constant on the endpoints: both map to the base point. -/
theorem loop_endpoints : loop 0 = loop 1 := by
  rw [loop_zero, loop_one]

/-- **Recursion principle for the circle.** An interval map `f` whose two endpoints
agree (`f 0 = f 1`) induces a map out of the circle. -/
def rec' {X : Type v} (f : unitInterval → X) (h : f 0 = f 1) : Circle → X :=
  Quot.lift f (fun a b r => by cases r; exact h)

/-- Computation rule at the base point. -/
@[simp]
theorem rec_base {X : Type v} (f : unitInterval → X) (h : f 0 = f 1) :
    rec' f h base = f 0 := rfl

/-- Computation rule along the loop. -/
@[simp]
theorem rec_loop {X : Type v} (f : unitInterval → X) (h : f 0 = f 1) (t : unitInterval) :
    rec' f h (loop t) = f t := rfl

/-- Uniqueness of the recursor: any map agreeing with `f` along the loop equals the
recursor. -/
theorem rec_unique {X : Type v} (f : unitInterval → X) (h : f 0 = f 1)
    (g : Circle → X) (hg : ∀ t, g (loop t) = f t) : g = rec' f h := by
  funext x
  induction x using Quot.ind with
  | mk t => exact hg t

/-- Every point of the circle is the loop at some interval point. -/
theorem loop_surjective : Function.Surjective loop := by
  intro x
  induction x using Quot.ind with
  | mk t => exact ⟨t, rfl⟩

end Circle

/-! ## The cubical torus

The torus is the quotient of the square that glues opposite edges: the bottom edge to
the top edge, and the left edge to the right edge. -/

/-- The gluing relation for the torus: identify opposite edges of the square. -/
inductive TorusRel : (unitInterval × unitInterval) → (unitInterval × unitInterval) → Prop where
  | horiz (x : unitInterval) : TorusRel (x, 0) (x, 1)
  | vert  (y : unitInterval) : TorusRel (0, y) (1, y)

/-- The cubical torus: the square with opposite edges glued. -/
def Torus : Type := Quot TorusRel

namespace Torus

/-- The canonical square map into the torus. -/
def mk (p : unitInterval × unitInterval) : Torus := Quot.mk _ p

/-- Endpoint behaviour on the horizontal edges: the bottom and top edges are glued. -/
theorem mk_horiz (x : unitInterval) : mk (x, 0) = mk (x, 1) :=
  Quot.sound (TorusRel.horiz x)

/-- Endpoint behaviour on the vertical edges: the left and right edges are glued. -/
theorem mk_vert (y : unitInterval) : mk (0, y) = mk (1, y) :=
  Quot.sound (TorusRel.vert y)

/-- **Recursion principle for the torus.** A square map `f` that agrees on opposite
edges induces a map out of the torus. -/
def rec' {X : Type v} (f : unitInterval × unitInterval → X)
    (hh : ∀ x, f (x, 0) = f (x, 1)) (hv : ∀ y, f (0, y) = f (1, y)) : Torus → X :=
  Quot.lift f (fun a b r => by
    cases r with
    | horiz x => exact hh x
    | vert y => exact hv y)

/-- Computation rule for the torus recursor. -/
@[simp]
theorem rec_mk {X : Type v} (f : unitInterval × unitInterval → X)
    (hh : ∀ x, f (x, 0) = f (x, 1)) (hv : ∀ y, f (0, y) = f (1, y)) (p : unitInterval × unitInterval) :
    rec' f hh hv (mk p) = f p := rfl

/-- Uniqueness of the torus recursor. -/
theorem rec_unique {X : Type v} (f : unitInterval × unitInterval → X)
    (hh : ∀ x, f (x, 0) = f (x, 1)) (hv : ∀ y, f (0, y) = f (1, y))
    (g : Torus → X) (hg : ∀ p, g (mk p) = f p) : g = rec' f hh hv := by
  funext x
  induction x using Quot.ind with
  | mk p => exact hg p

/-- The square map is surjective onto the torus. -/
theorem mk_surjective : Function.Surjective mk := by
  intro x
  induction x using Quot.ind with
  | mk p => exact ⟨p, rfl⟩

/-- The torus, as the product of two circles, by sending a square point to the pair of
its circle coordinates. -/
noncomputable def toCircles : Torus → Circle × Circle :=
  rec' (fun p => (Circle.loop p.1, Circle.loop p.2))
    (fun x => by simp [Circle.loop_zero, Circle.loop_one])
    (fun y => by simp [Circle.loop_zero, Circle.loop_one])

/-- The inverse map from `Circle × Circle` to the torus. -/
def ofCircles : Circle × Circle → Torus := fun p =>
  Circle.rec'
    (fun x => Circle.rec' (fun y => mk (x, y)) (mk_horiz x))
    (by
      funext c
      induction c using Quot.ind with
      | mk y => exact mk_vert y)
    p.1 p.2

theorem left_inv (t : Torus) : ofCircles (toCircles t) = t := by
  induction t using Quot.ind with
  | mk p => rfl

theorem right_inv (p : Circle × Circle) : toCircles (ofCircles p) = p := by
  obtain ⟨c1, c2⟩ := p
  induction c1 using Quot.ind with
  | mk x =>
    induction c2 using Quot.ind with
    | mk y => rfl

/-- The torus is equivalent to the product of two circles. -/
noncomputable def torusEquivCircles : Torus ≃ Circle × Circle where
  toFun := toCircles
  invFun := ofCircles
  left_inv := left_inv
  right_inv := right_inv

end Torus

end CubicalSemantics

# Future Directions

The following freeform directions extend the concrete quotient model of basic
cubical shapes developed for the circle and torus.

## 1. A dependent eliminator for the quotient circle

The present development supplies only the non-dependent recursor `Circle.rec'`,
which covers maps `S¹ → B`. The natural next step is a dependent eliminator that,
given a motive `P : S¹ → Type`, a point `b : P base`, and a loop datum identifying
the two transported endpoints, produces a section of `P`. The key insight is that
the dependent case forces us to make the endpoint transport *explicit*, because in
a set-theoretic model there is no native transport — the user must supply the
identification `b = b` along the loop as data, exactly as a HIT eliminator would
demand. Why now? Because we already have a clean `Quotient.lift`-based
non-dependent recursor whose computation rule is `rfl`, so the dependent version
can be prototyped against a known-good baseline and its extra coherence obligations
isolated cleanly rather than discovered by trial and error.

## 2. Filling the torus square with explicit 2-cells

Our torus carries a meridian and a longitude that are independent by `rfl`, but the
model has no native notion of a path between paths, so the commuting square that a
genuine `T²` requires is currently absent. The key insight is that, in a quotient
model, a `2`-cell is itself just a quotient of the unit *square*
`unitInterval × unitInterval` by a boundary-gluing relation, so the same
explicit-relation recipe that built `S¹` should build the filler directly. Why now?
Because the one-dimensional case is fully worked out and axiom-audited, so the
two-dimensional boundary bookkeeping can reuse the exact same `Quot.sound` pattern
and be validated incrementally instead of all at once.

## 3. Computing a set-theoretic fundamental group

It is unclear how much homotopical content survives when continuity is dropped: the
loop exists and is non-degenerate as data, but without topology the usual
winding-number argument is unavailable. The key insight is that, in this discrete
model, the "fundamental group" should be reconstructed combinatorially as the free
structure generated by the loop modulo the explicitly imposed endpoint relations,
turning a topological invariant into a purely algebraic quotient. Why now? Because
the loop and its endpoint identification are already formalized and their axiom
footprint is minimal, giving a concrete object on which to test whether the
algebraic reconstruction is faithful or collapses to the trivial group.

## 4. A uniform pushout recipe for explicit gluing

The circle arises by gluing the two endpoints of an interval, and many further
shapes (suspensions, spheres, wedges) arise by analogous gluings. The key insight
is that all of these are instances of a single quotient-of-a-coproduct pattern, so
a generic `Pushout` construction parameterized by an explicit span relation would
subsume the circle's gluing relation as one special case.

modules.demo:
"""
Numerical / computational demonstration of the set-level quotient model of the
cubical circle (S^1) and torus (T^2).

This script mirrors the Lean development:

  * The cubical interval is modeled by floats in [0, 1].
  * The circle S^1 is the interval with endpoints 0 ~ 1 glued.
  * The torus T^2 is the square [0,1]^2 with opposite edges glued.
  * Each space carries a recursion principle (eliminator) that requires the
    "toll" equations enforced by the gluing.
  * We exhibit the equivalence T^2 ~= S^1 x S^1 via explicit mutually inverse
    maps `to_circles` and `of_circles`, and verify the round-trip identities
    numerically.

Everything is self-contained and uses only the standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, Tuple, TypeVar

X = TypeVar("X")

EPS = 1e-12


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical interval and its endpoints
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def in_interval(t: float) -> bool:
    """Membership test for the unit interval I = [0, 1]."""
    return -EPS <= t <= 1.0 + EPS


I0: float = 0.0  # the 0 endpoint
I1: float = 1.0  # the 1 endpoint


def endpoints_ne() -> bool:
    """Proposition `endpoints_ne`: the two endpoints are distinct."""
    return abs(I0 - I1) > EPS


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical circle  S^1 = I / (0 ~ 1)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# A point of S^1 is represented by a canonical interval representative in [0, 1),
# i.e. we normalize the endpoint 1 down to 0, since loop(1) = loop(0) = base.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Circle:
    """A point of the cubical circle, stored as a canonical representative."""
    rep: float  # canonical representative in [0, 1)


def loop(t: float) -> Circle:
    """The canonical interval map (loop) into the circle.

    Sends every interval point t to its class; the endpoint 1 is identified
    with 0 (the gluing 0 ~ 1), realizing loop_zero / loop_one / loop_endpoints.
    """
    assert in_interval(t)
    if abs(t - 1.0) <= EPS:
        return Circle(0.0)
    return Circle(t)


BASE: Circle = loop(0.0)  # the base point = common image of the two endpoints


def circle_rec(f: Callable[[float], X], h: bool) -> Callable[[Circle], X]:
    """Recursion principle `Circle.rec'`.

    Given an interval map f : I -> X whose endpoints agree (the toll
    h : f(0) == f(1)), induces a map S^1 -> X with computation rule
    rec(loop t) = f t  and  rec(base) = f 0.
    """
    if not h:
        raise ValueError("circle_rec: endpoint toll f(0) = f(1) not satisfied")

    def induced(c: Circle) -> X:
        return f(c.rep)

    return induced


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The cubical torus  T^2 = (I x I) / (opposite edges glued)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Torus:
    """A point of the cubical torus, stored as a canonical square representative."""
    x: float  # canonical first coordinate in [0, 1)
    y: float  # canonical second coordinate in [0, 1)


def torus_mk(p: Tuple[float, float]) -> Torus:
    """The canonical square map into the torus.

    Glues bottom~top  ((x,0)~(x,1))  and  left~right  ((0,y)~(1,y))  by
    normalizing each coordinate's endpoint 1 down to 0.
    """
    x, y = p
    assert in_interval(x) and in_interval(y)
    nx = 0.0 if abs(x - 1.0) <= EPS else x
    ny = 0.0 if abs(y - 1.0) <= EPS else y
    return Torus(nx, ny)


def torus_rec(
    f: Callable[[Tuple[float, float]], X],
    hh: bool,
    hv: bool,
) -> Callable[[Torus], X]:
    """Recursion principle `Torus.rec'`.

    Given a square map f together with the two edge tolls
    hh : f(x,0) == f(x,1)  and  hv : f(0,y) == f(1,y),
    induces a map T^2 -> X with computation rule rec(mk p) = f p.
    """
    if not (hh and hv):
        raise ValueError("torus_rec: edge tolls not satisfied")

    def induced(t: Torus) -> X:
        return f((t.x, t.y))

    return induced


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The equivalence  T^2 ~= S^1 x S^1
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def to_circles(t: Torus) -> Tuple[Circle, Circle]:
    """`toCircles`: a torus point goes to its (longitude, meridian) pair."""
    return (loop(t.x), loop(t.y))


def of_circles(pair: Tuple[Circle, Circle]) -> Torus:
    """`ofCircles`: a pair of circle points reassembles a torus point."""
    c1, c2 = pair
    return torus_mk((c1.rep, c2.rep))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_circle_endpoints() -> None:
    print("=== Circle: endpoint gluing (loop_zero / loop_one / loop_endpoints) ===")
    print(f"  endpoints_ne (0 != 1 in I)?  {endpoints_ne()}")
    print(f"  loop(0) == base ?            {loop(0.0) == BASE}")
    print(f"  loop(1) == base ?            {loop(1.0) == BASE}")
    print(f"  loop(0) == loop(1) ?         {loop(0.0) == loop(1.0)}")
    print()


def demo_circle_rec() -> None:
    print("=== Circle recursion principle (rec_base / rec_loop) ===")
    # f(t) = cos(2 pi t) has f(0) = f(1) = 1, so it descends to the circle.
    import math
    f = lambda t: round(math.cos(2 * math.pi * t), 10)
    toll = abs(f(0.0) - f(1.0)) <= 1e-9
    g = circle_rec(f, toll)
    for t in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75):
        print(f"  g(loop({t})) = f({t}) = {g(loop(t))}")
    print(f"  g(base) = f(0) = {g(BASE)}")
    print()


def demo_torus_edges() -> None:
    print("=== Torus: opposite-edge gluing (mk_horiz / mk_vert) ===")
    samples = [0.0, 0.3, 0.7]
    horiz = all(torus_mk((x, 0.0)) == torus_mk((x, 1.0)) for x in samples)
    vert = all(torus_mk((0.0, y)) == torus_mk((1.0, y)) for y in samples)
    print(f"  mk(x,0) == mk(x,1) for all sampled x ?  {horiz}")
    print(f"  mk(0,y) == mk(1,y) for all sampled y ?  {vert}")
    print()


def demo_equivalence() -> None:
    print("=== Equivalence  T^2 ~= S^1 x S^1  (left_inv / right_inv) ===")
    torus_pts = [torus_mk((x, y))
                 for x in (0.0, 0.2, 0.6)
                 for y in (0.0, 0.4, 0.9)]
    left_ok = all(of_circles(to_circles(t)) == t for t in torus_pts)
    print(f"  ofCircles(toCircles(t)) == t  for all sampled t ?  {left_ok}")

    circle_pairs = [(loop(x), loop(y))
                    for x in (0.0, 0.2, 0.6)
                    for y in (0.0, 0.4, 0.9)]
    right_ok = all(to_circles(of_circles(p)) == p for p in circle_pairs)
    print(f"  toCircles(ofCircles(p)) == p  for all sampled p ?  {right_ok}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_circle_endpoints()
    demo_circle_rec()
    demo_torus_edges()
    demo_equivalence()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
